inputs.need:
I am a general practitioner and the prescribing lead for a primary care network of 11 practices in a district where many adults have no regular dentist. Every week our GPs see people with toothache or facial swelling, and in a notes search of three practices we found that 123 of 212 dental pain consultations over six months ended with an antibiotic prescription, often without any dental treatment planned. Antibiotics do not treat most dental pain, and the local microbiology team keeps asking us to reduce this.

We would like to run a cluster randomised trial across the network: practices would be allocated to a dental pain pathway (a short decision aid for GPs, a same-day telephone triage line run by the community dental service, and analgesia advice) or to usual care. The aim would be to reduce antibiotic prescribing for dental pain without increasing emergency attendances for dental infection. The community dental service has agreed in principle to run the triage line for 12 months.

I need help with the outcome definitions, how to count consultations and prescriptions from practice systems, how many practices and months we need, how to make sure patients with spreading infection still get antibiotics quickly, and whether we need individual consent from patients when the allocation is at practice level. Our practice teams are stretched, so anything that adds work during consultations will not be used.

records.title: A decision aid for dental pain in general practice and antibiotic prescribing: a cluster randomised trial
records.authors: Halvorsen-Mbatha J, Price-Okonkwo L, Varga-Tennant S
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 24 general practices to a one-page decision aid for dental pain with access to urgent dental advice, or to usual care, for 12 months. Among 4,310 dental pain consultations, antibiotic prescribing fell from 61 to 38 percent in intervention practices and from 60 to 55 percent in control practices. Hospital admissions for dental infection within 14 days were 0.4 percent in intervention practices and 0.5 percent in control practices. Repeat consultations for the same problem did not increase. The intracluster correlation for prescribing was 0.06. Practices were self-selected and had better access to dentists than average.

records.title: Antibiotics for toothache caused by pulpitis or apical periodontitis in adults: a systematic review of placebo-controlled comparisons
records.abstract: We searched four databases for placebo-controlled comparisons of systemic antibiotics for adults with toothache from irreversible pulpitis or acute apical periodontitis. Six small trials with 412 participants were included. When dental treatment was also provided, antibiotics did not reduce pain or swelling compared with placebo at 24 or 72 hours. No trial studied people who could not obtain dental treatment. Adverse effects were more common with antibiotics. Certainty was low because of small samples and imprecision. The review supports reserving antibiotics for spreading infection or systemic signs.

records.title: Same-day dental telephone triage for people presenting to general practice with toothache: first-year service data
records.abstract: A community dental service ran a same-day telephone triage line for patients referred by general practices with toothache. In its first year the line took 1,140 calls. Dental nurses booked 62 percent of callers for urgent dental care within 48 hours and gave self-care and analgesia advice to 29 percent. Antibiotics were advised for 9 percent, mostly for facial swelling or fever. The abstract does not state the year of the service data, the number of practices involved or what happened to patients who were not booked. No comparison with prescribing before the line opened is reported.

records.title: Management of acute dental problems for prescribers who are not dentists
records.abstract: This guidance leaflet for doctors, nurses and pharmacists covers toothache, dental abscess, ulcers and dental trauma. For toothache without swelling it recommends analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen and referral for dental treatment. Antibiotics are recommended only for spreading infection, systemic signs such as fever, or when urgent dental treatment cannot be obtained and infection is present. Red flags for same-day hospital referral include difficulty swallowing, trismus and swelling extending to the eye or neck. The leaflet gives no publication date, and its evidence sources are not listed.

records.title: Adults without a regular dentist and dental consultations in general practice: a population analysis
records.abstract: We linked a population survey of adults to practice consultation data in one region. In the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods, 38 percent of adults had no regular dentist, compared with 17 percent in the least deprived fifth. Adults without a regular dentist were three times as likely to consult a general practitioner for dental pain in a year. Among these consultations, antibiotic prescribing was more common where the nearest dental practice accepting new patients was more than 10 kilometres away. The survey response rate was 46 percent.

records.title: Why general practitioners prescribe antibiotics for toothache: an interview study
records.abstract: We interviewed 21 general practitioners about consultations for dental pain. Most described prescribing antibiotics because patients could not get dental care, because they feared missing a spreading infection, or because patients expected a prescription after waiting to be seen. Several said they lacked confidence in examining the mouth. Doctors wanted a direct route to same-day dental advice and a short decision aid that fitted into a ten-minute consultation. Some worried that declining antibiotics would lead patients to attend emergency departments instead.

records.title: Emergency department attendances for dental infection after changes in access to dental care
records.abstract: We examined emergency department attendances for dental abscess and facial swelling over three years in which the number of dental practices accepting new adult patients fell. Attendances rose by 24 percent over the period. Admissions for spreading dental infection remained rare at about 0.3 per 10,000 adults per year but were concentrated in adults without a regular dentist. Most attenders had seen a general practitioner or pharmacist in the week before. The analysis could not link attendances to earlier antibiotic prescriptions.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; two have no stated year and were left unrated. A cluster randomised trial found that a decision aid with urgent dental advice lowered antibiotic prescribing for dental pain without more admissions for dental infection, and a review of placebo-controlled trials found no benefit of antibiotics when dental treatment was given. General practitioners prescribe mainly because patients cannot reach dental care, a problem concentrated in deprived neighbourhoods. A triage line booked most callers for urgent care in one service report whose date and follow-up are unknown. Evidence supports testing the pathway locally with a safety balancing measure.
response.gradeRationale: One cluster randomised trial in better-served practices and a review of small trials; indirect to a district with poor dental access; two sources undated and unrated.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; two left unrated with unknown year; five claims; certainty low.

response.reading: Prescribing for dental pain is driven by lack of dental access and fear of missing infection rather than by expected benefit, which trials show is absent when dental treatment is given. A pathway that supplies same-day dental advice addresses the driver directly. The main risk is that fewer antibiotics could delay treatment of spreading infection, so emergency attendance must be watched. Deprivation shapes both dental access and prescribing.

response.overview: Two-arm cluster randomised trial in 11 general practices over 12 months, comparing a dental pain pathway with usual care, using routinely coded data.
response.population: All consultations by adults aged 16 or over coded for dental pain, toothache, dental abscess or facial swelling of dental origin in the 11 practices from January to December 2027.
response.exposure: Intervention practices: a one-page decision aid in the clinical system, a same-day telephone triage line run by the community dental service, and a printed analgesia advice sheet. Control practices: usual care.
response.procedures: Practices are allocated by a statistician outside the network, stratified by list size and deprivation fifth. The data team extracts coded consultations, prescriptions within 3 days and emergency attendances monthly. A safety group reviews emergency admissions for dental infection every three months.

response.designSummary: Two-arm cluster randomised trial, 11 practices, 12 months, analysis at consultation level accounting for clustering.
response.sampleSize: The network search suggests about 140 dental pain consultations per practice per year. With a baseline of 58 percent, an intracluster correlation of 0.06 as in the retrieved trial and 5 or 6 practices per arm, the design effect is about 9.3, giving roughly 80 percent power to detect a fall to 38 percent at two-sided alpha 0.05. A smaller fall, to 45 percent, would need about twice as many practices; if the observed intracluster correlation is higher, a neighbouring network would have to join.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of prescription within 3 days on arm, with practice as a random effect and the stratification variables as fixed effects; small-sample corrected confidence intervals.
response.secondaryAnalysis: The same model for repeat consultation; emergency attendance and admission for dental infection reported as counts and rates per 1,000 consultations by arm, with the safety group's review; prescribing by deprivation fifth.
response.missingData: Outcomes come from coded records and are complete for consultations that are coded; coding completeness is checked against a sample of free-text notes in two practices.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary and balancing measures are reported with intervals.
response.software: R (lme4 with small-sample corrections); analysis plan finalised before data extraction.
response.summary: About 80 percent power for 58 to 38 percent with 11 practices; smaller effects would need more practices.

response.risks: Low: the pathway follows existing guidance; the risk is delayed antibiotics for spreading infection, managed by red flag advice and the safety review.
response.consent: Allocation is at practice level and outcomes come from routine records; a waiver of individual consent has been requested and the ethics committee has not yet decided. Practices give organisational consent; patients are informed by practice notices and may opt out of data use.
response.data: Pseudonymised extraction by the network data team; no free text leaves practices except the coding check sample, which stays within the practice.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people without a regular dentist, in deprived neighbourhoods or with limited English are most affected. Allocation is stratified by deprivation, the triage line offers interpreters, and outcomes are reported by deprivation fifth.
response.effectiveness: A fall in prescribing without more emergency attendances would justify commissioning the pathway.
response.efficiency: Uses routine data and an existing dental service.
response.costs: Triage line staffing is met by the community dental service; data extraction within the data team's role.
response.grants: A small stewardship grant could fund independent statistical support.
response.partnerships: Community dental service, microbiology team, local dental committee and a patient panel from the network's participation group.
response.rebPath: Regional research ethics committee review under ICH-GCP and the Ottawa Statement on cluster trials; the waiver of individual consent is pending, and no allocation happens before the committee decides.
response.limitations: Few clusters; coded data may miss some consultations; the triage line exists only for 12 months.
response.summary: Cluster trial with a pending consent-waiver decision, a safety review and equity-stratified allocation.

response.partnershipPlan: Three members of the network's patient participation group, one without a regular dentist, review the analgesia sheet and the practice notices.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the community dental service's complaint themes are shared in anonymised form.

response.title: A dental pain pathway to reduce antibiotic prescribing in general practice: protocol for a cluster randomised trial

response.methods: Practices allocated in strata by size and deprivation; routine coded outcomes; mixed-effects analysis; independent safety review.
response.results: No data have been collected yet.

response.limitations: Few clusters; reliance on coding; one district.
